title: Count a heap of overlapping hex nuts one at a time on a desk tally counter
instruction: Count the hex nuts from the heap in the bin into the empty tray on the tally counter: zero it first, then lift the nuts out one at a time and click once for each.
context: Loose fasteners sit in parts bins as heaps, and a stock count is made by lifting them out one at a time and clicking a tally counter once for each, because a heap cannot be counted by eye. Stockers and order fillers (O*NET 53-7065.00, about 2.8 million US workers): "Receive and count stock items, and record data manually or using computer." The hard part is physical: taking one nut cleanly off an overlapping heap, where nuts lie across each other and hide the ones below, with the open fingers fitted between its neighbours, without lifting a second nut with it or knocking one out of the bin; a double pick or a dropped nut breaks the count. The other hand zeroes the desk counter by its knob and clicks its sprung key once per nut.
setup: Positions are on the table top, measured forward from the line through the two arm bases and left (+) or right (-) of the midline between them; the arm bases are 610 mm apart. Nothing else is on the table. 1) Tally counter: a desk tally counter matching the Redington Model 18 desk tally (13-1804) in size and controls: chrome-plated steel case on a black ABS base plate (57 mm across, 5 mm thick), bolted to the table with the base centre 240 mm forward and 120 mm right; 66.5 mm tall overall. Its round case (46 mm across, 29.6 mm deep) has a 28 x 7 mm window facing the robot with four figure wheels (white 4 x 2.3 mm figures on black drums, 7 mm apart); it shows 0038. On top is a 10 mm round push key with a 7 mm stroke; one full stroke adds 1. On the case's right side is a reset knob, 13 mm across, standing 20 mm out from the case on a horizontal axis 31 mm above the table; turning its top away from the robot by 55 to 70 degrees returns the units and tens wheels to 0, and a spring returns the knob. The maker publishes neither key travel nor reset turn: here the key counts once pushed past 4.25 mm (about 2.5 N), and one 55 to 70 degree twist zeroes the count where the Redington knob is turned until all wheels read 0 (up to a full turn). The README gives every part, spring and size needed to build this counter. 2) Bin: a blue polypropylene parts tray, 163 mm front to back, 171 mm wide, 33 mm tall, 3 mm walls and floor, fixed with its centre 262 mm forward and 225 mm left. 3) Tray: a white polypropylene tray of the same build with 25 mm walls, fixed and empty, centre 98 mm forward and 115 mm left. 4) Eleven DIN 934 M16 hex nuts, zinc-plated steel, 24 mm across flats, 27.7 mm across corners, 13 mm thick, 16 mm bore, 33.3 g each, in one overlapping heap in the middle of the bin, every nut lying flat and turned at its own angle: six on the bin floor in two rows of three (about 38 mm apart along a row, the rows about 52 mm apart, at about 197 and 249 mm left, from 218 to 295 mm forward); four lying across pairs of neighbouring floor nuts, two on each row; one on top, lying across the two on the row nearer the midline, its top 39 mm above the bin floor. Seen from above one nut is almost entirely hidden and seven are partly covered. The README lists every nut's centre, layer and turn; a printed template under the bin floor places the floor layer.
scoring: A nut is in the bin while its centre is inside the bin's inner wall rectangle (157 x 165 mm) and at most 50 mm above the table, and over the tray under the same rule for the tray. N is the number of nuts over the tray that rest there: the nut's lowest point within 2 mm below to 3 mm above the tray floor top, or its centre above the outline of a nut already in N with its lowest point between that nut's mid-height and 3 mm above that nut's top (a nut held over the tray with nothing under it does not count). M is the number of nuts not in the bin. A nut is lifted while it is neither in the bin nor over the tray. The counter shows a valid reading only while the units and tens wheels are both within 6 degrees of a figure; the latched reading R is the last valid reading the wheels showed for 0.25 s, starting at the counter's 0038. Sticky faults (once one happens the score is 0 for the rest of the trial): dropped (a nut centre outside both trays' outer footprints and less than 20 mm above the table, or more than 20 mm below the table top anywhere); two lifted (two nuts lifted at the same moment); out of step (after R first shows 0000, R and M differ by 2 or more at any moment: one click goes with each nut, made before or after it is moved). No credit unless R has been 0000 at some moment. Released: every gripper TCP at least 30 mm from each nut's bounding box and from the bounding boxes of the key and the reset knob. At rest, over the last 1 s: each nut within 1 mm and 2 degrees of its current pose and slower than 1 cm/s; both wheels within 2 degrees of a figure and each varying by at most 0.3 degrees; the key within 0.5 mm of its top stop and varying by at most 0.2 mm; the knob within 2 degrees of its rest stop. With no fault: 1.0 = all 11 nuts in the tray (N = 11), R = 11, the wheels showing 0011 now, released and at rest. 0.8 = N = 11 and R = 11, but not released, not at rest or the wheels between figures now. 0.25 = N = 11 and R = 10 or 12 (one missed or one extra click that never left R 2 away from M). 0.4 x N / 11, rounded to 3 decimals = 1 <= N <= 10 and R = N (an accurate but unfinished count). 0 otherwise: the untouched start, a sticky fault, no steady 0000, N = 11 with R off by 2 or more, or a partial count with R other than N. Success is 1.0 held for 1 s.
reset_notes: Use zero object jitter. Rebuild the heap from the README's pose table (floor layer on the template, then the four nuts across them, then the top nut), the tray empty, the counter on 0038, the key up and the knob on its rest stop. Nothing is consumed. The scorer's latched reading, its 0000 and fault flags and its 1 s windows start fresh each trial.
fidelity: Counter internals (pawl, detents, heart-cam reset) are our design after a 1951 patent; stroke and spring forces are estimates; only the units and tens wheels turn. Figures are 7 mm apart (real 5) and the knob stands 20 mm out (real 8) so the pads can pinch it. Quick presses can slip (a carry did at 75 mm/s). Counter bolted down; friction 1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic. The heap is a fixed set of flat-lying nuts from a pose table; a heap tipped from a bag would also have tilted nuts. More in the README.
